item.title: Space X and Tesla exploring merger, CEO Elon Musk says
item.description:
SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger — and Elon Musk thinks "it's a good idea," the CEO of both companies said Tuesday.

Why it matters: SpaceX and Tesla have increasingly been collaborating on chips and AI projects — and Musk leads both companies — prompting widespread speculation that they could join forces.

Driving the news: Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call that the two companies have formed committees of independent directors to explore the possibility of a deal.

  • "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions," he said, but he added that "I think it would be a good idea."

Zoom in: Musk said "there's a lot to be gained" from cooperation on technologies like AI, chips, robotics and connectivity.

  • But he said a deal is not certain.
  • "I think that would be overstating it," he said, noting that 50% of Tesla shareholders would need to approve the deal, which he called a high hurdle.

What they're saying: Tech analyst Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management said he believes there's a 95% chance a deal will take place in the next two years.

  • "Believe me, shareholders would support this," Munster said Tuesday on X after Musk made his comments.

Of note: Any combination would be massive: SpaceX has a market cap of more than $2 trillion, while Tesla's is nearly $1.5 trillion.

  • Tesla reports its quarterly results on Wednesday.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Exclusive: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio
item.description:
OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building AI agents to help pharmaceutical companies manage drug development, the ChatGPT maker shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: Rival AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are both pushing into science as they look to expand beyond their core competencies in coding and cybersecurity.

State of play: OpenAI will integrate Orchestra's team and technology into Rosalind, its suite of AI models and tools designed for life sciences researchers, the company said.

  • Orchestra's platform allows scientists to delegate tasks like monitoring studies, tracking drug development timelines and identifying potential delays to AI agents.
  • Both companies aim to deploy agents that can connect scientific findings with the decisions and next steps required to advance potential treatments.
  • Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Between the lines: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity, they want to say they are responsible for, say, curing cancer, solving math, and fundamentally changing every critical industry in the world.

  • Those ambitions have fueled acquisitions from rival AI labs.
  • Anthropic acquired AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April, according to The Information.

Zoom in: OpenAI introduced its specialized GPT-Rosalind model in April to help researchers tackle complex problems in biology, chemistry and drug discovery.

  • OpenAI has also partnered with pharmaceutical giants including Novo Nordisk and Moderna to bring AI into research and development workflows.
  • OpenAI says developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, a timeline it hopes AI can shorten.

Zoom out Anthropic has been making its own aggressive push into life sciences.

  • In June, Anthropic launched Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform that connects scientific databases, analysis tools and specialized agents.
  • In September, the company announced a new biological research lab and said Claude had helped discover a previously unknown enzyme system with similarities to CRISPR, though some scientists said these finders were overblown, per Bloomberg.

The bottom line: The AI race is shifting from building the best models to applying that intelligence across industries.

  • Several AI investors told Axios a key question as AI companies go public is how far they can expand into new markets.

item.title: Homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low
item.description:
The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing.

The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century.

  • New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards.

By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said, to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows.

  • Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023.
  • Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001.
  • Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday.

State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000.

  • That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out.
  • In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector.
  • Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters.

Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all signs point to it getting worse, not better.

  • For all the bipartisan emphasis on increasing housing supply — most prominently in the passage of a law to encourage more building earlier this year — conditions are weighted against a building boom.
  • Housing developers are competing with data center builders for labor and materials like copper, concrete and HVAC equipment.

Of note: Restrictionist immigration policy has also crimped the supply of construction workers.

  • "Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work," said NAHB chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, in the sentiment release.

Between the lines: An unfortunate side effect of relying on Fed interest rate policy for macroeconomic stabilization is that interest-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, take it on the chin when the economy shows signs of overheating.

  • It's particularly problematic now, when persistent undersupply of housing is a defining economic challenge of our age.

The bottom line: The current alignment of interest rates, housing supply and construction costs isn't making anybody happy.

  • Builders can't afford to build, buyers can't afford to buy, and even the people sitting pretty with pre-2022 mortgages can't afford to move.

item.title: How the energy crisis could become a food security crisis
item.description:
The Iran war and the Ukraine-Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds.

Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies.

  • The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more.
  • The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic.

Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund.

  • Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region.
  • "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned.

State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes.

  • "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm.
  • "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states.

Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds.

The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention.

  • The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive.
  • "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food."

Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate the overlapping threats.

  • Middle Eastern prices for exported sulfur, a fertilizer ingredient, reached a record $1,000 per metric ton in July, after starting the year at a historically high $500 per metric ton.
  • 47% of the global sulfur trade normally goes through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • In Indonesia, industrial use of palm oil, largely for biodiesel, is expected to be roughly five times its 2015-16 level.

The bottom line: A global food crisis is by no means certain.

  • But if wars keep disrupting energy and fertilizer supplies, and weather cuts harvests in key regions, "the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place," S&P warns.

item.title: AI takes on great experiment in self-rule
item.description:
Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact.

  • With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth.

Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good.

  • In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending.

The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring.

  • Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves.
  • These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption.
  • At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies.

Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth.

  • Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and employee pledges, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are earmarked for the public good.
  • Musk: The people. Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by urging the company to give shares "directly to the public." On Monday, Musk pledged to give every American child a share of SpaceX next year — a staggering $10.5 billion giveaway at current prices. Musk called it the "first of many," though he offered no details on how the unprecedented distribution would work.
  • OpenAI: The government. CEO Sam Altman has floated giving the U.S. government a 5% stake in OpenAI through a sovereign wealth fund — potentially handing Washington a multibillion-dollar interest in one of the world's most powerful AI companies. Altman envisions an Alaska-style fund that could distribute the industry's investment returns directly to Americans, though the plan remains preliminary and would likely require congressional approval.

Reality check: The numbers are staggering. So are the assumptions about future wealth, billionaire follow-through and the public's willingness to trust its benefactors.

  • Bill Gates and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge in 2010, a voluntary promise by billionaires — including Musk — to give away most of their fortunes. Gates built a philanthropic empire, only to become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories.
  • Anthropic's ambitions depend on extraordinary growth projections — its own employees envision 17% GDP growth in 2030 — while Musk has a history of making spectacular promises that fail to materialize.
  • Anthropic's roots in effective altruism, a philosophy deeply distrusted by the Trump administration and its allies, also raise a more fundamental question: Who gets to define the public good?

Between the lines: No industry requirements or consensus exist on how best to redistribute their expected wealth. But Trump Accounts — which allow families, businesses and individuals to invest in tax-advantaged funds for children — are emerging as a favorite vehicle for free-market AI leaders.

  • Billionaire investor Brad Gerstner, a driving force behind the program, is championing a vision of broad-based ownership in which ordinary Americans share directly in the economic upside of the AI revolution.
  • SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in July pledged roughly $320 million in company shares to 2 million children through Trump Accounts — a potential blueprint for distributing an even larger slice of Musk's fortune.

What to watch: The Trump administration hasn't fully relinquished its regulatory authority, potentially complicating the emerging experiment in AI self-governance.

  • After Anthropic disclosed that its AI had submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police and improperly interacted with government websites, the White House declared that AI companies must report security incidents and remedy any harm.
  • "This notification and remediation process is not optional," Trump's Super Intelligence Force warned — a striking assertion of federal authority just weeks after the president blessed a voluntary system of industry oversight.

Axios' Zachary Basu and Bradley Olson contributed reporting.

item.title: The budget deficit swells, while the cost of debt rises
item.description:
Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred, U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures.

Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession.

  • The deficit is being driven in part by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war.

By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data.

  • That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion).

Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates — a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021.

  • Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget.

The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office.

  • At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking President Bush's infamous "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing re-election.
  • Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts.

What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called bond vigilantes might still press for it.

item.title: "Power is probably the forever bottleneck": Grid delays threaten the AI race.
item.description:
Silicon Valley moves fast and breaks things, but the U.S. electrical grid moves slowly and requires permits.

  • The explosive growth of AI is colliding with the glacial pace of building out new power infrastructure, prompting a new warning from Goldman Sachs that energy bottlenecks are set to stall the AI race.

Why it matters: Amid a wave of anxiety from Wall Street about the debt-fueled AI buildout, Goldman points to power as the biggest risk to trillions in spending in a new report shared exclusively with Axios.

Driving the news: Goldman expects global data center power demand to surge 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from the U.S., according to the report.

  • "Power is probably the forever bottleneck," Jason Tofsky, Goldman's global head of digital infrastructure investment banking, noted in the report.
  • The bank estimates roughly $7.6 trillion in capital spending between 2026 and 2031 across computing, data centers and power infrastructure.

Zoom in: The physical infrastructure needed to support AI is moving far more slowly than the technology itself.

  • The U.S. has roughly 2,600 gigawatts of proposed power generation and storage projects awaiting grid connections, more than twice the grid's existing installed capacity, though many projects may never materialize.
  • The median time from an application for a grid connection to commercial operation is roughly five years.

Between the lines: The so-called AI race, which has long been defined by advances in frontier AI models, is really about who can get their hands on enough power, Goldman argues.

  • That could mean a longer, less predictable buildout, delayed financial returns and greater risks for companies investing heavily before securing power.

Follow the money: The massive expansion is being financed with debt, raising the stakes if construction timelines slip.

  • Goldman projects $420 billion in global hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027, up more than 60% from its 2026 estimate.
  • Debt is expected to finance roughly 35% of hyperscaler capital expenditures next year.
  • And hyperscalers account for just 40% of AI ecosystem credit fundraising, underscoring how widely the borrowing extends.

The intrigue: Since January, 86 projects have been canceled or significantly delayed, including 76 directly linked to local opposition, according to Goldman.

  • Put together, this paints a picture of extended delays.

Yes, but: Slower deployment could also help prevent over-investment by giving actual demand time to catch up with spending.

Meanwhile: The boom is transforming utilities from traditionally slow-growing businesses into major beneficiaries of AI investment.

  • Utility capital plans are expected to reach $1.3 trillion between 2026 and 2030.
  • Tech giants are considering arrangements to directly fund the power generation, transmission lines and electrical infrastructure their data centers require.

The bottom line: If you build AI systems, users will come, but they can only stay if there's enough power to go around.

item.title: I let agents plan a WNBA Finals trip (but kept my wallet to myself)
item.description:
Let's call it the Battle of the Bots, part 1: I decided to put two of the newest personal AI agents, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, through their paces, with the WNBA Finals providing a natural testing ground.

Why it matters: AI companies are racing to create the digital assistant we turn to for everything from shopping to travel planning. But there's still a gap between what these agents can do and what I'm comfortable letting them do.

  • They also need to pass what we'll call "The Human Benchmark": that is, can they do something as fast, or as well, as a human? The answer is ... not quite yet, but the capabilities are still impressive.

The big picture: For the test, I asked each assistant to plan a fantasy trip to Atlanta to see my beloved Golden State Valkyries, organize a purple-themed brunch watch party and create souvenir programs.

  • I also had them help me shop for Valkyries merch, which eventually turned into a side quest for WNBA basketball cards.

The cost: Muse is free for most uses, with optional $20 and $100 monthly subscriptions. Dots requires a ChatGPT Pro subscription, starting at $100 monthly, or access through a business or enterprise plan. More on Dots.

Where they shined: Both agents were surprisingly good at handling complicated, multistep assignments.

  • When I asked them to find flights and tickets for Game 3 in Atlanta, both caught that the game had been moved up a day and that tickets weren't yet on sale to the general public. The available seats were being offered through the resale market, likely at inflated prices.
  • Both found good flight options. Muse opened a browser and let me enter my information to try to sign up for a ticket presale.
  • Dots, meanwhile, flagged a scheduling conflict with an enrollment fair, which it gleaned from my AI-assisted effort to keep tabs on the joys of finding the right high school in San Francisco.

Where they were creative, but imperfect: Both agents could turn broad instructions into surprisingly elaborate finished products, though neither was quite ready to replace a human editor.

  • For my purple-themed brunch, Muse designed a colorful 10-page recipe booklet featuring ube waffles and lavender-honey butter. Dots produced a more practical eight-page packet with detailed cooking instructions and attention to dietary preferences.
  • Muse's shopping list called for 12 eggs, while its recipes required 13. Both agents also designed invitations that needed aesthetic and language edits before I'd send them to friends.
  • Both menus were far more elaborate than anything I'd actually make for a basketball watch party. Left to my own devices, I'd probably just buy some purple-frosted donuts.

Another creative test: I asked both agents to create a 1980s-style WNBA Finals souvenir program, then later to turn my photos from Game 1 into a keepsake.

  • Dots' 38-page vintage program was more visually engaging, with player photos, graphics and extensive statistics. Muse's 35-page version was less attractive but had some fun touches, including a fictional computer ad and an advertisement for my imaginary brunch.
  • Both programs contained questionable statistics. Muse later sent an unsolicited update correcting several factual errors.
  • For the photo program, Dots delivered a 12-page version in just 47 seconds, while Muse took considerably longer. It did, however, suggest an interesting photo spread highlighting different generations of Valkyries fans.

Where they struggled: Actually doing things. I asked both agents to help me buy Valkyries merchandise, eventually settling on WNBA trading cards.

  • Both helped compare options and prices. I chose Target, where my store credit card offered a 5% discount and free shipping.
  • Muse attempted to complete the purchase but got stuck at Target's sign-in page. Dots instead directed me to the Target app, where my account and payment information were already saved.
  • Dots' less automated approach turned out to be faster, even though both services support purchases with user approval.

The trust problem: Both agents could have done more if I'd been willing to give them greater access to my accounts and wallet. I'm not yet comfortable authorizing purchases of hundreds or thousands of dollars, or at a point of trusting them enough for consequential decisions.

The bottom line: For me, the sweet spot for these agents is doing the research and legwork while leaving me to make the final decisions.

  • P.S.: I couldn't actually make the Atlanta trip or host the brunch because of other commitments. But I did end up buying three boxes of WNBA basketball cards. You know, for research.

item.title: Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America
item.description:
Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year.

Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift.

What they're saying: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday.

  • He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant.
  • He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens.

By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S.

  • If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion.
  • Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings.

Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX.

  • In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts, a gift now worth nearly $300 million.

Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more.

  • Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with background details.

item.title: How AI giants will reshape global philanthropy
item.description:
The AI boom is about to rewrite the rules of global philanthropy, shifting its center of gravity to Silicon Valley, where the IPOs of AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI will create the world's largest charitable organizations.

Why it matters: Rather than massive donations earmarked for renaming hospital wings or university graduate programs, expect the new wave of giving to mirror startup culture: flexible capital, ambitious bets and a search for measurable impact.

Driving the news: Anthropic announced Sunday that it plans to launch a massive benefit fund with 5% of its shares.

Zoom in: The company's pledge — which would amount to $100 billion if it reaches a value of $2 trillion in its IPO — will go to a public benefit fund and is set to grow as its valuation rises.

  • Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned LLC, giving it flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or distribute money directly to specific populations.
  • The commitment builds on the pledges of co-founders to give away 80% of their equity. A program available to early Anthropic hires and used by a large number of company staffers matched donations at a 3:1 ratio. The company says roughly half its employees participate in donation matching.
  • The company says the fund's shares will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or abroad.

The big picture: Anthropic is joining OpenAI, which is controlled by a nonprofit foundation that holds a 26% equity stake in the company, worth about $130 billion based on the company's current valuation. The foundation has the power to appoint OpenAI's board.

What they're saying: Anthropic says much of its public-benefit work — including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research and discounts for nonprofits and scientific institutions — will continue inside the company.

  • The new fund is intended to make other kinds of giving possible at greater scale, the company says.
  • Anthropic cited AI's effects on the labor market as one potential use and said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue, but that "bolder approaches may be needed."
  • Anthropic has not specified what those approaches would be, or whether the fund would make direct payments to workers affected by AI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's founders and some employees have close ties to effective altruism, a movement ostensibly dedicated to directing resources toward causes where they may do the most good.

  • Effective altruism has come under sharp criticism from the Trump White House, which has emphasized aspects of the movement that are far from the philanthropic mainstream.
  • Those include an acute interest in animal welfare, as well as seemingly abstract ponderings about the value of life, including comparing that of an infant to an adult, or future people to present people.
  • In an X post, Taylor Budowich, a former White House official, highlighted one such comment from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2010, when he said in a blog post that an adult death is "perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant's death."
  • Budowich also shared a few other "insane beliefs of those who make up Anthropic and how they think about prioritizing charitable giving."

The bottom line: Anthropic's fund — and the charitable giving of a massive new cadre of millionaires and deca-millionaires — could become one of the largest vehicles for new giving.

  • The bigger change may come with a new generation of Silicon Valley donors aiming to reset the agenda of modern philanthropy.

item.title: The AI attack-ad nightmare is coming true
item.description:
AI is producing reality-bending midterm ads about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a "Death to America" playing card.

Why it matters: The warnings about deepfakes are coming true. Election laws haven't kept pace with a world where campaigns can put words in opponents' mouths and create realistic-looking scenes that didn't happen.

  • The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans.
  • Four states have laws prohibiting certain uses of AI-generated deepfakes in political ads, while 27 more require some form of disclosure about their use.
  • No federal law specifically regulates AI-generated political ads.

The big picture: An Axios analysis found numerous political ads partly or fully made by generative AI, sometimes undisclosed.

Georgia Senate: Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, has run a series of AI-generated deepfake ads depicting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff getting beauty treatments.

  • The ads mock Ossoff's reported campaign spending on hair and makeup, saying he "talks pretty" but has "an ugly record" and "a lot to cover up."
  • Ossoff said in a C-SPAN interview: "It is deeply troubling to see ... deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising. And it's a slippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate, and the ad should come down immediately."
  • The ads don't disclose AI use, which Georgia law doesn't require.

Michigan Senate: A super PAC called Front Line Action used AI in an ad depicting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo with podcaster Hasan Piker and four women wearing niqabs.

  • Another AI-generated scene has El-Sayed playing a Risk-style board game with his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, and Piker. It depicts cards bearing statements that include "Death to America," "Do not Celebrate Thanksgiving" and "Celebrate 9/11."
  • The group has defended the ad, telling CNN it is "grounded in El-Sayed's own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign."
  • The ad features both a written and spoken disclosure that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence."

New York governor: Republican Bruce Blakeman's campaign and allied super PACs have repeatedly used generative AI in ads attacking Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, with varying degrees of disclosure.

  • One AI-generated ad released by the Blakeman campaign depicts the Tooth Fairy struggling to come up with cash to give to children, saying she "just can't afford to be the Tooth Fairy in Kathy Hochul's New York."
  • Another Blakesman spot says onscreen: "We asked AI what a truthful Kathy Hochul ad would look like." The ad features AI-generated scenes of Hochul attending an upscale dinner and standing outside a police precinct while a man asks her: "Want some crack?"

Pennsylvania governor: A new ad from Republican candidate Stacy Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro talking about taxes, abortion and data centers.

  • The spot puts this quote in his mouth: "This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers. Fact is, I was the one who fast-tracked data centers right here in PA, right after they handed me $5 million in political contributions."
  • Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder, in a statement to Axios, dismissed the ad as "cheap, dishonest AI bullshit."

Texas Senate: Democratic candidate James Talarico has been a consistent target of AI-generated ads from both Republican Ken Paxton's campaign and outside super PACs.

  • A Paxton campaign ad uses AI to depict Talarico defacing a Bible with crayon and saying, "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were."
  • Talarico told NBC he "tried in the legislature to ban AI deepfake videos in political campaigns because they are misleading. They are lying about a candidate in this race."

Kentucky's 6th District: No Going Back PAC, backed by President Trump's MAGA Inc., has run several ads using AI to boost Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado.

  • One ad features multiple AI-generated deepfakes of Democrat Zach Dembo, including one scene in which he stares into the camera.
  • "I expected them to lie about my record, but I did not expect them to lie about my appearance," Dembo said in a statement to Axios, adding that "using AI to create fake or misleading images is the beginning of a very dangerous path for our democracy."

item.title: The overlooked geography of American poverty
item.description:
Data: U.S. Census; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data.

Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account.

  • Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture.

What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%.

  • The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average.
  • California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure, or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%.
  • Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%.

How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography.

  • The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs.

Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%.

  • Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate.
  • Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025.

Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate.

  • Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses.
  • The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller.

The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

item.title: Exclusive: Musk tells Isaacson "AI and robots" will need to fix deficit
item.description:
Elon Musk tells biographer Walter Isaacson in a new podcast interview that the fizzled DOGE experiment, which the SpaceX and Tesla CEO once headed, proved there's "no way we were gonna solve the deficit from within the government."

  • "The only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots," Musk tells the author for a new podcast series, "The Builders with Walter Isaacson," premiering Tuesday. "We're not gonna solve it by trying to save our way there."

Why it matters: Musk's comments to Isaacson — author of the definitive 2023 biography, "Elon Musk" — admit that DOGE was a flop, but point to the chance that some future administration will take a new stab at the problem using ever-more-capable AI.

Zoom in: Musk said the appetite to cut spending "is not there at the presidency, the House, the Senate or the judiciary. Basically, no one in authority in the government whatsoever — with maybe a few rare exceptions [like the] Rand Pauls of the world — actually wants to reduce spending."

  • "Maybe if the president made that his primary goal, we could do that," Musk added. "If you try to solve the deficit and stop wasteful spending, you make a lot of enemies. President Trump likes to be liked. He doesn't like people calling him, being upset about ... some funding being stopped."

Musk admits he "kinda got carried away, basically" and that he wound up being "gone for too long" from his companies.

  • "What I should have done," he added, "was be more in the background ... and probably only had it last for a month or two" rather than the four months he was formally in the White House.
  • "I should have gone back and focused on AI a little sooner than I did."

When Isaacson asked Musk if his time in the West Wing had been too seductive, in a way, Musk replied: "It was, a little bit. I mean, it was kinda cool 'cause ... I'm just there in the Oval Office while all these, like, big momentous decisions are being made."

  • Asked about the time he brandished a chainsaw onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) a month into Trump's second term, Musk said: "That was a weird weekend."
  • Pressed to elaborate, Musk said: "Let's let sleeping dogs lie or whatever."

The big picture: Isaacson warned this week that Steve Jobs and the other great creators of the personal computer age would be cautious about autonomous AI agents not tightly connected to human control.

  • Isaacson includes his warning in the new preface to an updated edition, published this week, of his sweeping 2014 history of the digital age, "The Innovators: How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses, and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution."

Behind the scenes: Isaacson tells me he launched "The Builders" because he wanted to press the builders of this new AI age on these dangers and hear in their own voices what motivates them.

  • "Musk is an amazing engineer who is pushing us forward with Starship, Starlink, Neuralink, and autonomous EVs," Isaacson said. "But as I describe in my biography, I think he is too prone to darkness and conspiracies when it comes to politics and people. His complexities come through in the interview, as I hope they do in the biography."

What's next: Isaacson's podcast series, created by media company Kaleidoscope, includes conversations with Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, Fei-Fei Li, and Dario and Daniela Amodei.

  • A series preview says the tech legends "open up about their ambitions, what frightens them, how they think about humanity, and what drives them to build so big and so fast. The conversations are intimate, charming, and sometimes chilling."

Listen to a trailer for "The Builders."

item.title: That Y2K feeling: Why today's economy resembles 2000
item.description:
It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down.

The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026.

  • The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever.
  • And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001.
  • We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled.

Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure.

  • The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%.
  • GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth.
  • It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year.

Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May.

  • But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution.

What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000.

  • "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said.
  • "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings."
  • "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced."

Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today.

  • Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes.
  • But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher.

Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time.

  • That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down.
  • The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001.

Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery.

The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

item.title: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook.

Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong.

What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting.

  • Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
  • His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting.
  • "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok.

State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war.

  • Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear.
  • Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings.

Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services.

  • Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch.

Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy.

  • Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside."
  • Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one."

What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy.

  • The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

item.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
item.description:
Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyperpolarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum.

Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI, is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale.

Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting.

  • The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah).

The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging:

  1. Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes.
  2. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers.
  3. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock.

Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar.

  • The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews.
  • Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout.

State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry.

"I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about."

  • The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously."
Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence

The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes.

  • Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats.
  • Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans.
  • Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies.

By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest.

  • The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence.
  • A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer.

Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades.

  • Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells.
  • Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups.
  • Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections.

What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium.

  • "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said.

Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water.

  • Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity.
  • Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption.

What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar.

  • The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews.
  • Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout.

State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry.

  • The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously."
Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence

The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes.

  • Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats.
  • Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans.
  • Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies.

By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest.

  • The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence.
  • A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer.

Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades.

  • Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells.
  • Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups.
  • Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections.

What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium.

  • "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said.

Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water.

  • Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity.
  • Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption.

What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

item.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
item.description:
Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone.

Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality.

Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns.

  • While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period.
  • More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace.
  • Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030.

Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multiday sell-off of its stock and debt.

  • Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf.

Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue.

  • It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times.
  • Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit.
  • Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: Approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion.

Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks.

  • Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI.
  • That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today.

Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize.

  • Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years.
  • At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs.

Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears.

  • The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period.
  • But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky.

The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about.

  • The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom.
  • If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

item.title: "Mommy and daddy" play nice: Apple and Meta team up to bring open-source Muse to Macs
item.description:
Apple and Meta, whose leaders have spent years trading barbs over privacy and the future of computing, are joining forces to bring one of America's most powerful open-weight AI models to Apple's high-end Macs.

Why it matters: The collaboration marks a striking detente between two longtime Silicon Valley rivals, underscoring how the AI race is reshaping relationships across the technology industry.

  • The companies still compete over devices and the next generation of computing, but both see an opportunity in bringing powerful AI capabilities to personal computers.
  • "We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again," Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios.

Driving the news: Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open, a model similar to Muse Spark 1.3 that it says is the most powerful U.S.-developed open-weight AI model available.

  • Meta joins a host of Western AI companies that have released powerful open-weight systems that promise to slash AI costs, provide companies with more control and offer an alternative to the Chinese AI ecosystem.
  • Nvidia on Tuesday released updated versions of its Nemotron family of models, and U.S.-based Reflection AI and France's Mistral both released new open-source models last week.
  • As proof of Muse Spark Open's capabilities, Meta worked with Apple to make the model run locally across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework.

Zoom in: The prospect of a powerful model — it has 816 billion parameters — running on Apple hardware offers a proof of concept for how companies could build their own AI systems.

  • That could give companies more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs and proprietary models from leading AI companies, potentially shifting some of the economics of AI.
  • Meta's model will be free to download, with a license allowing commercial use, and will also be available through cloud providers and developer tools.

What they're saying: Wang said the companies have been working together for several months, with Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive now at Meta, helping bring the two sides together.

  • "I think he played a really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together," Wang said in a telephone interview.

Flashback: Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have repeatedly clashed over privacy and their competing business models.

  • In 2018, amid Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal, Cook was asked what he would do if he were Zuckerberg. "I wouldn't be in this situation," Cook replied. Zuckerberg called Cook's comments "extremely glib."
  • The rivalry intensified in 2021, when Apple introduced new privacy protections that struck at the heart of Facebook's ad business. Zuckerberg reportedly told employees that Facebook needed to "inflict pain" on Apple over the dispute, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The big picture: The AI race is making for some strange bedfellows, scrambling long-standing Silicon Valley rivalries and even bringing together political adversaries.

  • Anthropic is leasing up to $15 billion per year of computing capacity from Elon Musk's SpaceX, even as it competes with his AI company.
  • Microsoft, OpenAI's longtime partner, is investing billions in rival Anthropic and incorporating its Claude models into its own products.
  • And in Washington, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders and MAGA strategist Steve Bannon have found common ground in calling for tougher AI safeguards and challenging the power of Big Tech.

Between the lines: The Apple-Meta collaboration doesn't mean the companies have resolved their differences, but it suggests those disagreements no longer prevent them from working together when their interests align.

  • Meta benefits from making its AI models widely available, while Apple can showcase the capabilities of its most powerful computers.
  • And because the model runs locally, Meta doesn't receive users' prompts or other information — sidestepping the privacy concerns that have long divided the companies.

"Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Wang said of how developers use the model.

Yes, but: Making powerful AI models openly available raises concerns that bad actors could remove safeguards and use the technology for cyberattacks or biological threats.

What we're watching: Whether the collaboration marks the beginning of a broader relationship between Apple and Meta.

  • For now, Apple is helping demonstrate that Meta's AI models can run locally on its computers. A more significant step would be Apple incorporating Meta's models into Apple Intelligence, giving the Facebook parent a role in powering Apple's own AI features.

The bottom line: Wang acknowledged that Apple and Meta will continue to compete in some areas, but said that doesn't have to prevent them from working together.

  • "Where it makes sense to collaborate and partner, we want to be able to do so," he said.

item.title: The too-hot-for-comfort economy
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply.

The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction.

  • There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response.

Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday.

  • Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher.
  • There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows.

Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years.

  • If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy.

State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28.

  • Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month.
  • Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control.
  • If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent."

The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down Thursday despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number Wednesday mostly reversed later in the trading session.

  • It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities.
  • The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number Wednesday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It was down to 4.72% Thursday morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data.

What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces Wednesday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note.

  • "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

item.title: CEO confidence drops into negative territory
item.description:
Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council; Chart: Axios/Emily Peck

CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, finds a survey out Thursday morning from the Conference Board.

Why it matters: Business leaders are mind-melding with most consumers, whose opinions on the economy are now lower than during the pandemic.

  • Such sour sentiment is shaping up as a key issue in the midterms just weeks away.

Where it stands: The CEO Confidence Index fell to 46 in the most recent period, down from 52 just three months ago — any number below 50 connotes negative sentiment.

  • The nonprofit Conference Board and the Business Council surveyed 131 Fortune 500 CEOs from Sept. 21-Oct. 5.
  • The survey measures how chief executives at major public companies feel about current economic conditions and their expectations for the economy and their own industries over the next six months.

By the numbers: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter.

  • Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago.
  • 94% of CEOs cited cybersecurity threats among their top AI-related concerns.

The surge in energy prices — particularly diesel, which is crucial to companies' energy costs — also contributed to the fall in sentiment, Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board, tells Axios.

  • "All these inflationary shocks, one after the the other, is weighing down on the confidence of both CEOs and consumers," she says.

Between the lines: The key worry when CEO moods darken is the spillover into the economy, as they pull back on spending and hiring.

Reality check: Despite their dimming views, CEOs have for the most part maintained their spending plans, per the survey.

Case in point: A separate survey also out Thursday morning found that 89% of U.S. CEOs said they expected to increase headcount over the next three years as AI creates more business opportunities.

  • "As we put more AI into our processes and platforms, the capacity opens up," Tim Walsh, the CEO of KPMG, which conducted the survey, told Axios' Nathan Bomey.
  • "What you're seeing there is CEOs being really optimistic that they can actually expand their business, which is going to result in a bigger workforce for them."

The bottom line: CEOs are gloomy about the economy, but their dark mood hasn't yet translated into a meaningful pullback in investment plans.

item.title: Anthropic brings Wall Street an AI bull case
item.description:
AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic on Wednesday made that case in cash.

  • The company presented eye-popping financials to investors, saying it was cash flow positive in the third quarter, with revenue surging nearly 50% to $16.8 billion compared with the April-to-June period.

Why it matters: As Wall Street broadly spent the day fearing an AI bubble, Anthropic offered what investors have been desperate to see: evidence that frontier AI can be a sustainable business.

State of play: The S&P 500 fell by more than 1% for the first time in 53 sessions, while Anthropic showed off a balance sheet that promises profitable AI, sources told Axios.

Zoom in: Consider just one of the stats reported by Anthropic: The company is cash flow positive even as some of the world's most profitable companies are struggling to keep their AI spending in check.

  • For context, Google parent Alphabet, long a money-printing machine, turned free cash flow negative in its second quarter as AI infrastructure investment soared.
  • Investing gurus — especially those focused on the frothiness of companies relative to their underlying value — have long seen free cash flow as a gold standard for the long-term health of a business.
  • Anthropic, a much younger company competing in the same expensive AI race, says it was cash flow positive in the third quarter. The Anthropic figures were first reported by the Financial Times.

Yes, but: The company's blistering pace of growth appeared to slow compared with the difference between the first and second quarters, when sales more than doubled.

  • Few investors saw growth as likely to continue at that pace, especially while the company faced ferocious competition from OpenAI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's latest financial disclosures reinforce what analysts and investors have been telling Axios:

  • The company's early bets on frontier intelligence and enterprise adoption are translating into meaningful financial gains that put it on track for the largest IPO in history. Some investors expect it to reach a $2 trillion valuation.

item.title: Scoop: "OG" Bill Gates returns to wage war on AI risks
item.description:
Bill Gates is gearing up to dramatically expand his AI safety push, personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: The formidable, sharp-elbowed Bill Gates who built Microsoft is back, and he's directing his competitive fire toward what he has come to see as one of the most important causes of his lifetime.

  • "I can reach CEOs on this better than you can," Gates told one person he consulted on AI safety, showing an eagerness for combat that associates say is a return to "OG" form.

Driving the news: Once a voice for optimism on AI, Gates has grown dismayed by an escalation of model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as insufficient regulation, sources say.

  • As he prepared to make the case for a far more robust regulatory framework on AI, he conferred extensively with leading AI executives, researchers and safety advocates, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
  • That process led Gates to see containing AI risks as one of the most important issues he will engage with in his lifetime, the people said.

Behind the scenes: People Gates has spoken to called his advocacy a "comeback tour," an attempt to rebuild a legacy that has been tarnished by his past association with Jeffrey Epstein.

  • Gates has said he's aware that some people may dismiss his warnings due to the Epstein ties.
  • "What I did do, in some ways, was very limited, and it was motivated by my desire to raise money," Gates told Axios in August. "But ... it was a huge mistake."
  • However, Gates sees the stakes as too high to stay on the sidelines and believes his Rolodex, foundational tech credibility and wealth can do an immense amount of good.

The big picture: This crusade marks a stark evolution for Gates, moving him from a measured optimist to an urgent alarmist.

  • Just three years ago, Gates assured the public that "the risks of AI are real but manageable." He viewed the technology's disruptions as historical parallels to the introduction of the PC or the internet and argued that society would adapt.
  • By August, his outlook had darkened considerably. In a sprawling essay, Gates warned that the current trajectory was volatile.
  • He sounded the alarm in an interview with Axios, indicating that the world is dangerously unprepared for the economic and societal upheaval ahead.

Zoom in: Gates' research has convinced him to step beyond essays and media interviews, although he has yet to define the exact contours of his campaign.

  • In his August essay, Gates called for new regulatory institutions capable of coordinating AI policy, reserving some jobs for humans and taxing AI usage and robots.

The stakes of the AI race have resurrected a version of the billionaire the tech world hasn't seen in decades. In recent interviews, he's shown flashes of the acid-tongued titan who ruthlessly built Microsoft, chiding journalist Ezra Klein for asking whether any regulation is needed beyond what Klein called "normal corporate reputational management."

  • Gates sarcastically made fun of a world where lawsuits are the only form of regulation. "Say you kill 100 million people. You want to use a lawsuit? I almost can't keep a straight face."
  • It is a jarring contrast to the softer, sweater-wearing philanthropist persona he has cultivated over the past 20 years.

What's next: Gates' calls for robust regulation will put him on a collision course with the Trump administration, which has favored a lighter regulatory touch, organizing a group of top officials to police the industry through a voluntary safety pact.

  • As Gates' plans crystallize, it remains to be seen whether AI safety becomes a defining battle of his late career.
